subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & cost levers — Acme AI
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alex Jordan <alex@acme-ai.com>
Cc: Priyom Das <priyom@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Thu, 25 Jun 2026 14:05:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & cost levers — Acme AI

Alex — thanks again for your time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned:

Call recap:
- Goal: Real-time assistant in Acme’s product for end-users (search + summarization).
- Target SLOs you called out: 95th percentile latency <= 400ms for the first token in streaming flows; p50 token latency < 80ms; sustain 1,200 QPS at peak with 200 concurrent active sessions.
- Streaming: server-side streaming required to render partial responses to the client within 150ms from first model token.
- Accuracy/quality: you prefer a strong open model (instruction-tuned) but are open to hybrid approach if cost/latency tradeoffs are favorable.

Primary constraints we heard:
- Latency is a blocker for UX; anything beyond ~500ms for initial content reduces engagement.
- Cost cap target (initial PoC): ~$15k/month for inference costs.

Suggested levers we discussed (high level):
- Continuous batching for high QPS: reduces per-token cost significantly while keeping tail latency bounded with smart deadline-based dispatch.
- Prefix / KV caching for repeated prompts and partial context re-use.
- Quantization profile: 4-bit or 8-bit quantization for most traffic, keep FP16 for high-fidelity queries.
- Model variants: smaller low-latency model for short replies/clarifying questions, larger model for longer summaries (auto-routing).
- Streaming optimization: push-first-token path and early flush for UI render, then background decoding for the remainder.

Proposed next steps:
1) I’ll share a short technical note with expected latency/throughput ranges per lever + rough cost delta (attached). (Action: Marissa)
2) Priyom (SE) will propose an initial PoC config we can stand up in a Dedicated pool — baseline + optimized config for A/B. (Action: Priyom)
3) Schedule a 30-min tech sync next week to lock target metrics for the PoC and agree on instrumentation.

Can you confirm the SLO numbers above match what you want us to optimize for? Also send any additional top-of-stack constraints (e.g., max allowed output tokens per response, region requirements).

Thanks,
Marissa Cole

From: Priyom Das <priyom@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alex Jordan <alex@acme-ai.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Fri, 26 Jun 2026 08:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLOs & cost levers — Acme AI

Alex / team — hi, Priyom here (solutions engineering). I put together a short technical breakdown below on realistic expectation bands and which levers move the needle most for each metric. This is intentionally high level; we can follow with numbers tailored to your actual prompt/seq-length distribution during the PoC.

1) Latency (first-token p95) — baseline bands (US-West, A100-class GPU):
- Baseline (no batching, FP16, 13B model): ~120-180ms p95 for first token at low concurrency (<50).
- With continuous batching and deadline dispatch: ~90-140ms p95 at 200 concurrent sessions (depends on batching window).
- With quantized kernels (4-bit) and optimized kernel selection: ~60-110ms p95.

Key levers: continuous batching (good), quantization profile (4-bit/8-bit), model variant (smaller model for short responses).

2) Throughput / concurrency — answers per second and active sessions:
- Streaming adds overhead per-active-session. For 1,200 QPS with 200 concurrent sessions (avg response length 200 tokens): you’ll want a Dedicated pool sized for sustained throughput with auto-burst for spikes.
- Batching + KV caching can reduce GPU token compute by 30-60% depending on cache hit rate.

Key levers: batching policy, KV/prefix caching, auto-scaling pool sizing, and model offloading for heavy tail requests.

3) Cost levers & rough deltas (order-of-magnitude estimates):
- Continuous batching: 20-45% per-token cost reduction for high QPS workloads.
- KV/prefix caching: 10-50% savings depending on reuse (search + summarization have high reuse for prompt prefixes).
- Quantization (4-bit path): 25-60% cost reduction vs FP16, with small quality delta for many workload types.
- Model routing (hybrid variants): use a 7B low-latency model for short clarifying exchanges and a 33B model for long summaries — 30-70% net cost savings compared to always using a single large model.

4) Streaming specifics & UI latency tricks:
- Push-first-token pipeline: prioritize first-token decode and send to client within a tight deadline; continue background decoding. This reduces perceived latency even when total generation time is larger.
- Early flush heuristics for partial sentences increase perceived responsiveness.

5) PoC recommendation (what we propose to provision):
- Dedicated pool: mixed instance sizes (A100-style) with 2 configurations: baseline and optimized.
- Baseline config: FP16, standard batching, no caching; measures your end-to-end latency baseline.
- Optimized config: continuous batching w/ 25ms batching window, KV cache enabled, quantized 4-bit path for 80% of traffic, model routing for short vs long responses.
- Instrumentation: p50/p95 token latency, time-to-first-token (server->client), cache hit rate, batch sizes, and token compute costs per route.

Next steps I need from your side to size PoC:
- Typical prompt length (tokens) and distribution (short/medium/long).
- Expected peak QPS and percent of traffic that needs streaming vs non-streaming.

If you want I can sketch a sample Dedicated pool config and a ballpark monthly cost for the baseline vs optimized config once you share a token distribution. Happy to meet Mon 10:30am PT — Marissa, can you confirm?

—Priyom Das
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
priyom@redwoodinference.com
